\section[generoso]{generoso — generous}

\label{lesson:ES-C723-generoso}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for cowardly, then the Spanish for to dare.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: generoso}
\textbf{generoso} — \textquotedblleft{}generous\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Mi tío es muy generoso con todos.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{My uncle is very generous to everyone.}
\end{quote}

\emph{Ser generoso con alguien}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{generoso} comes from Latin \emph{generōsus} \textquotedblleft{}of noble birth\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB), built on \emph{genus} \textquotedblleft{}birth, family\textquotedblright{}; noble birth was expected to give freely.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{generoso}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{generoso}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{generoso}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for cowardly, then the Spanish for to dare, then say \emph{generoso} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does generoso mean? (\textquotedblleft{}Generous\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[egoísta]{egoísta — selfish; the selfish person}

\label{lesson:ES-C723-egoista}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for to dare, then the Spanish for generous.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: egoísta}
\textbf{egoísta} — \textquotedblleft{}selfish; the selfish person\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
No seas egoísta y comparte.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{Do not be selfish, share.}
\end{quote}

Same form for men and women.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{egoísta} is built on Latin \emph{ego} \textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{} with the ending \emph{-ista}; the word probably came in through French \emph{égoïste}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{egoísta}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{egoísta}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{egoísta}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for to dare, then the Spanish for generous, then say \emph{egoísta} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does egoísta mean? (\textquotedblleft{}Selfish; the selfish person\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.

\section[la amabilidad]{la amabilidad — kindness}

\label{lesson:ES-C723-amabilidad}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for generous, then the Spanish for selfish.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: la amabilidad}
\textbf{la amabilidad} — \textquotedblleft{}kindness\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Gracias por su amabilidad.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{Thank you for your kindness.}
\end{quote}

A polite formula in letters and shops. The adjective is \emph{amable}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{amabilidad} is a learned borrowing from Latin \emph{amābilitās} (EtymDB), built on \emph{amābilis} \textquotedblleft{}lovable\textquotedblright{}, from \emph{amāre} \textquotedblleft{}to love\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{la amabilidad}
  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{la amabilidad}, once more
  \item \emph{Say it:} a sentence of your own with \emph{la amabilidad}
  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for generous, then the Spanish for selfish, then say \emph{la amabilidad} again
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
What does la amabilidad mean? (\textquotedblleft{}Kindness\textquotedblright{}.) Say it once more.

\section[tacaño]{tacaño — stingy, mean}

\label{lesson:ES-C723-tacano}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for selfish, then the Spanish for kindness.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: tacaño}
\textbf{tacaño} — \textquotedblleft{}stingy, mean\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
No seas tacaño y paga la cena.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{Do not be stingy, pay for dinner.}
\end{quote}

The opposite of \emph{generoso}. Feminine \emph{tacaña}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{tacaño} was borrowed from Italian \emph{taccagno} \textquotedblleft{}stingy\textquotedblright{} (EtymDB); further back the origin is not certain.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Say it:} \emph{tacaño}, once more

  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for selfish, then the Spanish for kindness, then say \emph{tacaño} again
\end{itemize}

\section[cruel]{cruel — cruel}

\label{lesson:ES-C723-cruel}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Spanish for kindness, then the Spanish for stingy.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: cruel}
\textbf{cruel} — \textquotedblleft{}cruel\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{quote}
Fue muy cruel con su hermano.
\end{quote}

\begin{quote}
\emph{He was very cruel to his brother.}
\end{quote}

Same form for men and women; plural \emph{crueles}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{cruel} is usually traced to Latin \emph{crūdēlis} \textquotedblleft{}hard-hearted, cruel\textquotedblright{} (Lewis \& Short), a word built on \emph{crūdus} \textquotedblleft{}raw, bloody\textquotedblright{}.
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={What you've built}]
One more word for telling, explaining and describing at B1.
\end{grammarlens}

  \item \emph{Recall:} say the Spanish for kindness, then the Spanish for stingy, then say \emph{cruel} again
\end{itemize}
